https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/libra.text: Military WMD Menu Introduction Systems Facilities Agencies Operations Countries Hot Documents News Reports Policy Budget Congress Links Intelligence Homeland Security Space Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) Economic and Defense Cooperation and Support for Ukraine's EU Integration: Kyrylo Budanov Met with Latvia's President, Prime Minister, and Minister of Defense President of Ukraine 10 September 2026 - 17:15 In Riga, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov met with President of Latvia Edgars Rinkēvičs, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, and Minister of Defense Raivis Melnis. During his meeting with the President, Kyrylo Budanov thanked him for Latvia's continued and consistent support for Ukraine. They discussed the security situation in our country and the region as a whole, Latvian-Ukrainian defense cooperation, and Latvia's support for Ukraine's integration into the European Union. They also discussed diplomatic efforts to achieve peace. "Latvia will continue to resolutely support Ukraine, both politically and in practical terms," Edgars Rinkēvičs emphasized. Kyrylo Budanov and Andris Kulbergs discussed economic and defense cooperation between Ukraine and Latvia. In particular, they discussed expanding the partnership between the two countries' defense industries and the importance of accelerating the delivery of energy equipment ahead of winter. Kyrylo Budanov said it was symbolic that the meeting took place at a car museum founded by Andris Kulbergs's father. Its collection includes cars that belonged to Stalin and Khrushchev, as well as Brezhnev's wrecked Rolls-Royce. "The old general secretary simply lost control of the car, and the Soviet system never managed to repair it because of its technological backwardness and lack of resources. Any empire built on illusions and aggression ends up the same way: wrecked, with no spare parts and no future. We keep working," the Head of the Office of the President noted. The meeting with Raivis Melnis focused on the security situation, continued defense assistance, and deepening cooperation in the defense industry. "Latvia remains steadfast in its support for Ukraine, providing domestically produced defense equipment, while Ukraine's combat experience contributes significantly to strengthening Latvia's National Armed Forces," the Latvian Minister of Defense emphasized.

Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Russia Ukraine says Russia bombed apartment block as birthday gift for Putin Building in Pryluky destroyed, killing nine people including three children, officials say, night before Russian president’s 74th birthday Luke Harding Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.14 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 07.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin, who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday. Ukraine’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 15 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said. Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Nine people died, including three children, officials said, with 38 people injured. Rescuers picked through the rubble in an attempt to find survivors. “Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky. It was an ordinary five-storey block of flats,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. He acknowledged that Ukraine was struggling to shoot down enemy ballistic missiles, and appealed to allies to provide US-manufactured Patriot interceptors. “Air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” he said. View image in fullscreen People carry a casualty after the attack on Pryluky. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The bombardment featured 70 ballistic missiles, as well as 46 jet-powered drones, which in recent weeks have been terrorising Ukrainians on a daily basis . Ukraine’s air force said it managed to down just over 80% of the fast-moving drones – an improvement on the previous average of 50% to 60%. Eleven regions were hit. Two people were killed in Kyiv, with other deadly strikes in the central cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia, where four civilians died. There was also extensive damage in Dnipro. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian generals had given Putin his favourite birthday present : “war crimes”. Moscow’s grim strategy of bombarding the country’s population so it capitulated would not work, he said. “The Ukrainian people are not going to give up, because it’s about Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state,” he said. The “ultimate” present would be a dock in The Hague, home to the international criminal court, where the Russian president would stand trial, Sybiha said. ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks Read more One resident in Kremenchuk said the attack happened early on Wednesday. The woman told Ukrainian media : “We were making tea in the morning. My husband was getting ready for work. And that was it. I found myself on the floor. What can I say? It was very scary.” Local people in Dnipro said a blast wave affected 16 buildings, blowing out doors and windows. One woman, Iryna, said her auto parts workshop had been hit for the sixth time. The ceiling collapsed in Wednesday’s strike, she said, with toilets, sinks and equipment damaged. “The explosion happened around three in the morning. We were sleeping at home. Everyone was scared, probably the whole city heard it. We will restore the shop and continue to work,” she told the Suspline channel . Zelenskyy said Ukraine had carried out its own long-range strikes on economic and military sites inside Russia. They included two oil complexes and a training ground in the ⁠Perm, ​Samara ‌and Astrakhan ‌regions.“These are ‌justified Ukrainian responses to ​all Russian attacks on ⁠our people,” ​he said. The president posted dramatic video of a burning oil tanker close to the southern resort city of Sochi. Russian officials said naval drones had hit the Liberian-flagged ship, adding that “crude oil was burning openly on the Black Sea”. Its Indian crew of 23 was rescued, they said. Both sides have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In recent weeks Russia has picked off vessels carrying Ukrainian grain, paralysing maritime traffic from Ukraine’s southern ports including Odesa. Earlier this week, a civilian cargo ship sank after a suspected attack by Russian drones in the Black Sea. Its crew is still missing. A second vessel carrying grain was also hit while sailing in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, said the Bulgarian prime minister, Rumen Radev. The search for survivors was called off on Wednesday, according to Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive ⁠Agency. “There are no ​traces of the sailors from the ‌first ship, and there will ‌be none,” he said. https://science20.com/hank_campbell/sir_.text: Science & Society Sir David Attenborough Tells The UN Global Warming Is Causing The 'Collapse Of Civilization' By Hank Campbell in Science 2.0 December 5, 2018 Opens in a new window Opens in a new window Opens in a new window In 2006, former Vice-President and global warming clarion Al Gore said we only had 10 years to stop CO2 emissions or it would be too late. More cynical people noted that he came up with that 10-year figure because it was two years from his rematch contest for U.S. President plus eight he expected to be in office. It's beyond me to know if that was ever his intent, but if it was, perhaps a Peace Prize and an Academy Award made political campaigning too petty. He never ran again. In 2006, former Vice-President and global warming clarion Al Gore said we only had 10 years to stop CO 2 emissions or it would be too late. More cynical people noted that he came up with that 10-year figure because it was two years from his rematch contest for U.S. President plus eight he expected to be in office. It's beyond me to know if that was ever his intent, but if it was, perhaps a Peace Prize and an Academy Award made political campaigning too petty. He never ran again. That doesn't mean his climate prediction was forgotten in pop culture. Sir David Attenborough suggests the 2016 catastrophe inflection point actually happened. Europe's favorite science documentary narrator informed the United Nations Climate Summit in Katowice, Poland that , "If we don't take action, the collapse of our civilizations and the extinction of much of the natural world is on the horizon." Looking around, that clearly isn't true. In California, there are fires and then mudslides, no different than any other year, the northeast has blizzards and heat waves, the south has hurricanes and tornadoes. Even the numerical projections about the future are the same as in the past, they are just farther out now. There are some crazy ones, a 7 degree temperature rise a short while ago, just like Mr. Gore posited a 20 foot high ocean rise at a conference I attended (and after criticism starting with me, retracted a few weeks later ). But climate creeps so maybe Attenborough will turn out to be right, the same way some people claim Nostradamus predicted everything - by being vague. Climate has changed throughout the history of earth. Great places to live became uninhabitable as nature wandered. Once we gained the ability to fly in the early 20th century, pilots making a run between Cairo and Baghdad saw something that should have been impossible. In the middle of the black desolate desert so inhospitable the Bedouins called it Bilad esh-Shaytan - the Land of Satan - was an outline of walls for what was eventually named the lost city of Jawa . Excavators found its ruins contained solid floors, canals, artwork, ceramic jars, surrounded by walls. Not today you won't. Credit: Rome "La Sapienza" University, the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Italian Ministry for University and Scientific Research The artwork showed cattle, the walls were likely to keep in domesticated animals. In a city of that 20 acre size, thousands of people could have lived there, and their animals also. Clearly no one moved to the terrible place it is now. It's not temperature, it's climate Later analyses of paleoclimate data found that the temperature in the region had stayed around the same since the end of the last Ice Age but it was much wetter in 3,000 B.C. This matched climate change in other areas. Even the Dead Sea was not always dead. When it changed, people likely stuck it out for a while, assuming it was just weather, but eventually it was abandoned as the desert that exists now came into being. That is why it was a mistake for Vice-President to promote the term "global warming." The data were not available to be certain it was really globally warmer in modern years (that it is warmer than the beginning of the Industrial Revolution isn't a debate) but climate change has always happened. If it hadn't, Jawa might be the world's New York City. But we're also no longer superstitious. We recognize now (well, most of us do) that nature is not a sentient cosmic being lashing out at us for having cars and flatscreen TVs, nature is just fickle. We will never again see 500,000,000 people die from Smallpox even though nature made that happen. We used to have mass famine in cycles but thanks to science the boom and bust of food production has flattened out. If the rest of the world were as pro-science as America, famine would disappear entirely. If climate change could not kill us 5,000 years ago, it certainly won't now, so Attenborough's intonation sounds vaguely primitive, especially for someone associated with science. He's an actor and believes in making a difference, so perhaps he is leveraging his voice while he can, nothing wrong with that, but to do so in a publicity stunt (he used a "People's Seat" at the U.N. meeting even though he is a celebrity) and to blame California wildfires on climate change, as he did, is just irresponsible, and it promotes doubt about the neutrality of science in other areas. We can't be surprised that Californians don't accept GMOs and vaccines at alarming levels when we tell them the wildfires they experience every year are caused by CO 2 emissions rather than poor land management ( we couldn't even replace an endangered trout required by law due to another law preventing a gas generator on public land ) and too little water for people who live in areas where it is naturally desolate. Because agriculture is so huge in California, most Americans don't realize that the bulk of the state would naturally be deserted. It gets so little water it can't support large numbers of people. That creates a tinderbox. Instead, we are told greedy Americans who want fresh produce out of season and have it shipped in on emissions-belching trucks cause fires to sprout up. Why should Californians, or anyone, trust any science if we engage in scaremongering about hot-button issues? CO 2 emissions have dropped in the last 20 years, we have some of the cleanest air in the world. The air is so clean that a few years ago EPA even defined air quality down and began promoting tiny particulate matter - so small it takes an electron microscope to detect it - as being the same hazard as actual pollution. No one believes it but California meteorologists dutifully put up the scary maps they get from California air quality boards , who only have jobs as long as there is a new crisis to prevent. Telling people to be afraid of particulate ghosts is feeding into superstitious beliefs about the natural world. Telling them we are doomed to a 7 degree Fahrenheit temperature rise , based on a numerical methodology so prone to error it would get people fired from any private sector engineering company, is not constructive. It is instead making people think climate researchers are the science equivalent of shock jocks out to get attention with ever more bombastic stunts. And that distrust bleeds over into medicine and energy and food and chemicals. There is no reason the supplements industry should be $25 billion or Dr. Oz should be on television except people have learned it's too much work to know who is engaged in public good and who is just raising money for their non-profit by getting attention in the New York Times prophesizing doom . The age of CO 2 is almost over, even if nothing has replaced the energy density of gasoline just yet. Activists are already looking for new targets; they seem to be so concerned about America's drop in CO 2 from energy ( the private sector dropped emissions 8 years ahead of the abandoned Clean Power Plan ) that they have attacked the methane that has replaced it - they have declared war on fracking, the natural gas they used to endorse. Enabling them because we dislike corporations or want to promote the belief that corporate science is not real science is not helping anyone. Every time we let a celebrity or an environmentalist make an unscientific claim because we support the underlying science they manipulated, an anti-vaxxer is born. And there is no one to blame but us. Photograph: Marko Đurica/Reuters Opinion Serbia The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power Editorial Two years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new era Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.48 EDT Share T his weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. The tragedy , killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country. Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution. On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history. For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities. Photograph: Marko Đoković/EPA As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat Viktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority. What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge towards the bottom of European corruption rankings. Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided. As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’s Serbia , like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.
